blocks.text: Remember that verbs generally have a subject and an object: the person or thing that performs the verb (the subject: **He* is reading a book'), and the person or thing that is receiving the action (the object: 'He is reading *a book**). Just as the subject of a verb is in the nominative case, and the object of the verb is in the accusative case, there can be an *indirect* object of the verb that goes in the *dative* case.

The indirect object refers to objects that are not being directly acted upon. For example, 'I wrote a letter to you' - 'I' is the subject, 'a letter' is the object, and 'to you' is the indirect object. Thus, in Russian, instead of saying 'to you', they say the word 'you' in its dative form: **Я пишу письмо *вам***. There are many common verbs that can have an indirect object, and most correspond with the English use of the word 'to':

Some of these verbs don't use 'to' in English (e.g., 'I'll ring you' is, in Russian, is 'I'll ring *to* you'), while others can either use it or omit it (e.g., we can say both 'Give it to him' and 'Give him it'). In general, the object given or spoken about is in the accusative, while the person to whom the object is given or spoken about is in the dative case.

In Russian, as in English, there are verbs which can have both the direct and indirect objects (говорить, писать, читать, etc.): *Я пишу другу письмо.* — I am writing my friend a letter. In Russian, the noun denoting the indirect object (другу) is in the dative case. The dative case is used mostly to denote the person to whom something is given, sent, told, shown, etc.:
In these instances the dative case answers the questions кому? чему? The question чему? (for inanimate nouns) is seldom used.

After the verb давать-дать the object given is in the accusative case; the person to whom the object is given is in the dative case: *Он даст словарь сыну.* After посылать-послать the object sent is in the accusative case; the person to whom the object is sent is in the dative case: *Я пошлю книгу брату.* After говорить-сказать the person to whom something is said is in the dative case: *Я скажу ему, что вы уже здесь.*
From the Wikibooks Russian textbook (CC BY-SA 4.0). From the DLI Grammar Reference Book. Lessons 28, 39.

exercises.q: Яков купил ___ (свой друг, dat. sg.) подарок.
exercises.prompt: Jacob bought a present for his friend.
exercises.why: **друг → другу** (dat. sg.). Masculine, animate, nominative singular in a consonant. Declines like DLI's студент — every singular form has the same endings (D. sg. студенту). Ending — (no ending) → -у.  **свой → своему** (dat. sg. m., agreeing with другу). A possessive — declines like DLI's мой. Ending -й → -ему.  Declension: sg. друг · друга · другу · друга · другом · друге; pl. друзья · друзей · друзьям · друзей · друзьями · друзьях.  Dative: 1. Masculine and neuter (except masculine in -а, -я): студенту, учителю, озеру, полю. 2. All feminine, and masculine in -а, -я: сестре, дяде, Марии, двери. — DLI, Lesson 28.  «Notice the similarity of the endings of the possessives to the form of «они».» мой · моё — моего — моему — моим — о моём; моя — моей — мою; мои — моих — моим — моими — о моих. — DLI, Lessons 47–48.  — Model words and rules from the DLI Grammar Reference Book; forms from the OpenCorpora dictionary (CC BY-SA 4.0).

exercises.q: Отдавай ___ (человек, dat. pl.) должное.
exercises.prompt: Give credit where credit's due.
exercises.why: **человек → людям** (dat. pl.). Masculine, animate; nominative plural люди. The form changes by more than its ending, so no single ending is given — see the declension below.  Declension: sg. человек · человека · человеку · человека · человеком · человеке; pl. люди · людей · людям · людей · людьми · людях.  «For the dative and the prepositional plural there are two kinds of endings for each case: -ам, -ами, -ах after a hard, a sibilant or a guttural consonant; -ям, -ями, -ях after a soft consonant, a «ь» or a vowel. The formation of these cases does not depend upon the gender of the noun, but only upon the sound preceding the ending.» — DLI, Lessons 42–45.  — Model words and rules from the DLI Grammar Reference Book; forms from the OpenCorpora dictionary (CC BY-SA 4.0).

exercises.q: Том так обозлился, что показал ___ (другой водитель, dat. sg.) средний палец.
exercises.prompt: Tom got so angry that he flipped off the other driver.
exercises.why: **водитель → водителю** (dat. sg.). Masculine, animate, nominative singular in -ь. Declines like DLI's учитель — every singular form has the same endings (D. sg. учителю). Ending -ь → -ю.  **другой → другому** (dat. sg. m., agreeing with водителю). Adjective type III, guttural (after г, к, х) — declines like DLI's русский (every form has the same endings, apart from the masculine nominative singular (and the inanimate accusative equal to it), which ends in -ой here, not -ий): D. русскому. Ending -ой → -ому.  Declension: sg. водитель · водителя · водителю · водителя · водителем · водителе; pl. водители · водителей · водителям · водителей · водителями · водителях.  Dative: 1. Masculine and neuter (except masculine in -а, -я): студенту, учителю, озеру, полю. 2. All feminine, and masculine in -а, -я: сестре, дяде, Марии, двери. — DLI, Lesson 28.  «All adjectives agree in gender, number and case with the noun they modify.» — DLI, Lesson 47.  «Masculine adjectives of the "hard" and "guttural" types have in the nominative the ending -ой if stressed: новый — молодой; русский — плохой, and retain the stress on the ending throughout the declension.» «The adjective «большой» belongs to the guttural type, in spite of its -ш-: большого, большому, большим, о большом.» — DLI, Lesson 47.  — Model words and rules from the DLI Grammar Reference Book; forms from the OpenCorpora dictionary (CC BY-SA 4.0).

Declension: sg. негодяй · негодяя · негодяю · негодяя · негодяем · негодяе; pl. негодяи · негодяев · негодяям · негодяев · негодяями · негодяях.  Dative: 1. Masculine and neuter (except masculine in -а, -я): студенту, учителю, озеру, полю. 2. All feminine, and masculine in -а, -я: сестре, дяде, Марии, двери. — DLI, Lesson 28.  «All adjectives agree in gender, number and case with the noun they modify.» — DLI, Lesson 47.  — Model words and rules from the DLI Grammar Reference Book; forms from the OpenCorpora dictionary (CC BY-SA 4.0).

exercises.why: **командир → командиру** (dat. sg.). Masculine, animate, nominative singular in a consonant. Declines like DLI's студент — every singular form has the same endings (D. sg. студенту). Ending — (no ending) → -у.  **полковой → полковому** (dat. sg. m., agreeing with командиру). Adjective type I, hard — declines like DLI's новый (every form has the same endings, apart from the masculine nominative singular (and the inanimate accusative equal to it), which ends in -ой here, not -ый): D. новому. Ending -ой → -ому.  Declension: sg. командир · командира · командиру · командира · командиром · командире; pl. командиры · командиров · командирам · командиров · командирами · командирах.  Dative: 1. Masculine and neuter (except masculine in -а, -я): студенту, учителю, озеру, полю. 2. All feminine, and masculine in -а, -я: сестре, дяде, Марии, двери. — DLI, Lesson 28.  «All adjectives agree in gender, number and case with the noun they modify.» — DLI, Lesson 47.  «Masculine adjectives of the "hard" and "guttural" types have in the nominative the ending -ой if stressed: новый — молодой; русский — плохой, and retain the stress on the ending throughout the declension.» «The adjective «большой» belongs to the guttural type, in spite of its -ш-: большого, большому, большим, о большом.» — DLI, Lesson 47.  — Model words and rules from the DLI Grammar Reference Book; forms from the OpenCorpora dictionary (CC BY-SA 4.0).
